name: CURRENT AFFAIRS
clue: After quizzing his whaling-captain cousin, Benjamin Franklin published one of the first charts of this warm Atlantic current.

name: FACE THE MUSIC
clue: At the 1824 premiere of his Ninth Symphony, a soloist turned this composer around so he could see the ovation he couldn't hear

name: WORLD CUP HISTORY
clue: In 1930 this nation of some 2 million people hosted the first FIFA World Cup and won it too

name: GOING THE DISTANCE
clue: This event's exact 26-mile-385-yard length traces to the 1908 London Games' course, Windsor Castle to the royal box

name: DAYS OF THE WEEK
clue: Thursday belongs to the thunder god Thor; this day of the week honors his one-eyed father

name: MEDICAL IMMORTALITY
clue: Cancer cells taken from this Virginia woman without her consent in 1951 became the first immortal human cell line, called HeLa.

name: UNCONQUERED
clue: Its crushing 1896 victory over Italy at Adwa let this highland empire stay independent throughout the Scramble for Africa.

name: PLANETARY NAMES
clue: Alone among the eight planets, this one takes its name from Greek rather than Roman mythology

name: BACK FROM THE DEAD
clue: Revived from liturgical use into an everyday spoken tongue, this ancient language became official in the new state of Israel in 1948.

name: ACCIDENTAL PRESIDENTS
clue: He's the only person to serve as both U.S. vice president and president without being elected to either office

name: EUROPEAN RIVERS
clue: Rising in Germany's Black Forest, this river touches 10 countries on its way to the sea — more than any other river on Earth

name: LOW POINTS
clue: Bathers bob like corks in this lake between Israel & Jordan, whose shore, about 1,400 feet below sea level, is Earth's lowest land

name: POSTHUMOUS POETS
clue: Fewer than a dozen of her poems appeared in print before her death in Amherst in 1886; nearly 1,800 surfaced afterward

name: BOXED IN
clue: In Hesiod, the gods crafted her as the first mortal woman; she unsealed a jar, loosing every ill but leaving hope inside

name: HIGH & DRY
clue: Astronomers prize the cloudless skies over this Chilean desert, the driest non-polar place on Earth and home to the ALMA observatory.

name: DOME IMPROVEMENT
clue: Built for Justinian in just five years, this vast domed church of Constantinople later gained minarets as a mosque.

name: CHEMICAL SYMBOLS
clue: Its symbol W comes from Wolfram, its German name; no metal melts at a higher temperature

name: NOBEL LITERATURE
clue: In 1913 this Bengali poet of 'Gitanjali' became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature

name: BELOW SEA LEVEL
clue: The shores of this hypersaline lake, bordered by Israel and Jordan, are the lowest dry land on Earth

name: PROOF POSITIVE
clue: In 1931 this Austrian logician's incompleteness theorems proved that arithmetic contains true statements no formal proof can reach.

name: HIGH FIVES
clue: On April 4, 1964, this band pulled off a Billboard first, holding all 5 of the Hot 100's top 5 positions at once

name: FIRST EMPERORS
clue: After unifying China in 221 B.C., he standardized script, coins, and axle widths; thousands of terracotta soldiers guard his tomb.

name: NOBEL PHYSICS
clue: Einstein's 1921 Nobel Prize cited his explanation of this effect, not his theories of relativity

name: AGE OF EXPLORATION
clue: After Magellan died in the Philippines, this Basque navigator sailed the Victoria home, completing the first circumnavigation in 1522

name: UNFINISHED BUSINESS
clue: This Austrian composer's Symphony No. 8, left with only two completed movements, is known simply as the 'Unfinished'

name: FOR THE RECORD
clue: 'Mary had a little lamb' were the first words this Menlo Park inventor recited into his new phonograph in 1877

name: A DARK & STORMY NIGHT
clue: Subtitled 'The Modern Prometheus,' this novel sprang from an 1816 ghost-story contest at Lord Byron's villa on Lake Geneva

name: THE PERIODIC TABLE
clue: Element 98, first created in 1950 at a university cyclotron, takes its name from the state where it was made

name: TREE'S COMPANY
clue: The Americas' only Portuguese-speaking nation took its name from a tree whose heartwood yields a flame-red dye

name: A BRUSH WITH HISTORY
clue: Jacques-Louis David painted the 1793 death of this radical French journalist, stabbed in his medicinal bath by Charlotte Corday.
